editorial_note: Saturday brought little fresh news, so this Afternoon edition carries ==five stories==, four of them from Friday evening and the night that this morning's edition did not carry. The window therefore reopens the overnight hours, back to the Special edition's close at 17:19 CET on 6 November, and is labelled as widened; nothing an earlier edition carried is repeated. The one story from Saturday itself is a New York Times investigation into ==Chinese firms cleared to handle Nvidia's H200 chips==. Google DeepMind published two working papers in which AI agents helped weaken legacy 1024-bit RSA, and Anthropic is reported to be pressing ahead with its listing. There is ==no new frontier model release== and no coding-agent launch worth carrying.

stories.headline: US cleared Chinese firms with empty offices and sanctioned ties to handle Nvidia's H200 chips, the New York Times reports
paragraphs: A Chinese company called ==New Matrix==, which the Commerce Department approved this year to assemble Nvidia's H200 chips into AI servers, lists an office in a Beijing industrial park that stands empty, the New York Times reported on Saturday. The building's directory does not include the firm, and the park's management agency told reporters it had no record of it.

According to Chinese corporate records cited by the Times, New Matrix was created 17 months ago and its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity fund the US government ==placed on a trade blacklist in 2024==. Two analysts who examined the records told the paper they believed the firm may be a front for companies associated with that fund.

A summary of the full report by FourWeekMBA says New Matrix is the second approved H200 handler with no apparent presence at its address, after Maginfra in September, and that roughly ==two dozen Chinese firms== appear to have been approved to buy or handle the chips. The Bureau of Industry and Security told the Times it carefully reviews all applications for national-security risks.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: the H200 sales were allowed on condition that every company in the chain passed a security review; a second licensee with no visible operations questions how that review is done, just as Congress prepares closer scrutiny of Nvidia's China links.
stories.caveat: The New York Times page was read only up to its opening section; the agency's response and the count of about two dozen licensees come from FourWeekMBA's summary of the full article, read through a Chrome-like TLS route after a 429 reply. The front-company view is that of two analysts; ==no charges or licence revocations== have been reported.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind says human-guided AI agents found two weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA
paragraphs: Google DeepMind announced on the evening of 6 November, Paris time, two working papers written with cryptographers Nadia Heninger and Emmanuel Thomé in which AI agents, supervised by researchers, attacked ==legacy 1024-bit RSA==. Both papers state that deployed RSA keys of ==2048 bits or more are not threatened==.

The first paper shows that the PKCS#1 v1.5 signing format stops adding protection once an attacker may submit more than about half a block of data, or a 64-byte digest at 1024 bits. It also reports a re-run of a published 1024-bit signature computation: the first root took ==391 CPU core-years, 3.5 times less== than the original, and two cooperating AI agents designed, ran and debugged it in under four days.

The second paper, dated 5 November, is theoretical. With a precomputation costing about one factorisation, each further 1024-bit key could be factored at about 1/58 of the usual cost, ==30 times less== than with the best earlier method for that budget. One model generated the proofs and a second checked them, with the algebra machine-checked in Lean 4.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: the practical risk is limited to old keys still left in devices and signing services, but the papers are a concrete case of AI agents moving a slow mathematical field in days rather than months.
stories.caveat: Both are ==working papers, not peer reviewed==. The factoring gain is a leading-order estimate with lower-order terms set to zero; no factorisation factory was built and no keys were factored.

stories.headline: Anthropic still plans to list before Thanksgiving and raise $80 billion to $100 billion, the Financial Times reports
paragraphs: Update to Friday's reports that prospective buyers were discussing a valuation of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion. Anthropic has no intention of delaying its listing, unnamed sources told the Financial Times, in a report LinkedIn News summarised early on 7 November. The company still plans to ==go public before the US Thanksgiving holiday== on 26 November.

According to the same report, Anthropic aims to raise ==$80 billion to $100 billion== at a valuation of ==$1.25 trillion to $1.75 trillion==. An earlier Wall Street Journal report had said Thursday's AI-led market sell-off raised investor doubts about the plan, with some wondering whether the offering would be postponed.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: the reported range still sits above the $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion buyers were discussing on Friday, so the price set during next week's marketing will show who gave way.
stories.caveat: Anthropic has announced no price range, share count or date. The FT article is paywalled and was ==not read directly==; its figures come from LinkedIn News's summary.

sources.label: LinkedIn News (summary of the Financial Times report)

stories.headline: TSMC weighs making advanced memory chips at Nvidia's request, The Information reports; Nvidia is also financing packaging capacity at SPIL
paragraphs: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has begun drafting plans to make an advanced memory chip, ==3D DRAM==, at the request of Nvidia, its biggest customer, The Information reported on Friday, citing two people with direct knowledge, according to Reuters. TSMC could build new factories or convert an existing plant, the report said; it was not clear when production would start.
A move into memory would put TSMC up against ==Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron== during an AI-driven memory shortage that has pushed prices up. TSMC and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters.

Separately, Reuters reported in a 6 November article on chip packaging that Nvidia is providing ==billions of dollars in financing== to expand CoWoS packaging capacity at Siliconware Precision Industries, a unit of ASE Technology, for new factory space and equipment, citing one unnamed industry executive.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: memory and packaging, not chip design, are now the bottlenecks on AI hardware, and Nvidia is spending to widen both, pulling its suppliers into markets they did not plan to enter.
stories.caveat: Both reports rest on ==unnamed sources==; neither TSMC nor Nvidia has confirmed them. The Information's article is paywalled and was read only through Reuters' account of it.

sources.label: Reuters, via the Kansas City Star

stories.headline: John Langford leaves Microsoft and says its AI Frontiers research group is over after a move into Microsoft AI
paragraphs: Machine-learning researcher John Langford wrote on his blog on 6 November that he has ==left Microsoft== and that ==AI Frontiers is over==. The roughly 50-person group inside Microsoft Research worked on agents, such as the Autogen framework and the Fara computer-use agent, and on new training methods.

Langford wrote that the group was moved into ==Microsoft AI in early September==, and that its leadership's philosophy is scaling and "aggressively not research". He said every other founding member of the group's leadership seems to have reached a similar conclusion, and that there will be no internships with the group next year.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: it is a first-hand account of a large lab choosing scale over exploratory research, and it removes one of the few Microsoft teams publishing on agent frameworks.
stories.caveat: This is ==one departing leader's account==; Microsoft has not commented on it, and the group's formal status and remaining staff are not described.
